transcript.text: I am the operations lead at a tour company. Each month I tell our local partners how many guides to reserve in each destination for the month after next. If I reserve too few, we hire freelancers at the last minute for about three times the price; if I reserve too many, we pay a small fee for each guide we do not use. My director asked me for a machine learning model that forecasts how many bookings we will receive per destination each month. The table I shared is our booking export up to late February 2026: one row per booking with the booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, whether it had free cancellation, and whether it was cancelled. I will use the result myself every month to fix the reservation. [shares bookings.csv]

I looked at your export before writing any of this: 1,500 bookings, booked between 2025-01-01 and 2026-02-24, travelling between 2025-01-16 and 2026-08-16, across five real destinations (Paris 317, Bangkok 304, Dubai 302, London 283, Istanbul 282) plus 12 rows under a destination called "TEST".

**The problem, as I see it**

Each month you commit a guide count per destination for a travel month two months away. Your director's wording — forecast how many bookings we will receive per destination each month — is not that quantity, and the gap between the two is where the money is.

**What needs care before any work starts**

A booking received in March is mostly for travel in June or later; it doesn't tell you how many people stand in front of a group in April. You need travellers who actually show up in a destination in a given month, counted the way it will be knowable when you must decide.

A plain count by travel month is unusable today, because later months are still being booked: August 2026 shows 8 bookings against April 2026's 78, and that is not a collapse. The fix is to count every travel month as it stood two months before it started — a snapshot rule that mirrors your decision moment. Median lead time is 86.5 to 98 days by destination, so a two-month snapshot already sees about two thirds of the eventual travellers, and 73 of April 2026's 78 bookings were already placed 60+ days ahead.

Guides follow non-cancelled bookings, and free cancellation makes that number move late.

The cost is asymmetric, so the number you reserve should not be the middle of the forecast. When a shortfall costs about three times a surplus, the useful output is an upper quantile of it. Which quantile depends on your idle-guide fee relative to a guide's price — I assumed the fee is small; tell me the ratio and I set the model to it.

Two honest limits: booking dates cover barely one full seasonal cycle (July 2025 at 141 travellers, August 2025 at 119, versus March 2026 at 109), so seasonality rests on one summer.

**Ways to solve it**

Analysis baseline now: month-of-year patterns per destination under the snapshot rule — fast, defensible, and it's the bar anything else must clear. A forecast model: same target, learned per destination-month and tuned to your cost ratio — slower, needs the fee, but it is what feeds the reservation. A decision sheet: skip modelling, reserve from booked-on-hand plus a historical uplift factor — least ML, most robust on one year of data. I'd build the model, but only after the baseline exists.

**The plan**

1. Clean: drop the 12 TEST rows and both identifiers, confirm `cancelled` is a 0/1 flag, and check why `price` arrives as categorical. Verified by row counts before and after each step.
2. Build the snapshot history: for each destination and travel month, count travellers booked as of 60 days before that month starts. Check that this explains most of the final travellers.
3. Set the target: net travellers at travel time, using each destination's cancellation behaviour. Check against actuals for the months now closed.
4. Baseline: seasonality plus level per destination, no ML.
5. Model: trained only on features knowable at the decision date (booked-on-hand, lead-time mix, channel and nationality mix, month of year), tuned to your asymmetric cost.
6. Validate strictly time-forward on the last fully observable months, and report the cost of errors, not just average error.
7. Hand you the monthly routine: what to run, what number to read, what to reserve.

Stop when the model's time-forward cost per destination-month is below the baseline's and you can reproduce the number yourself each month.
If a step fails: if the snapshot explains too little of the final travellers, we switch to the decision sheet; if the model doesn't beat the baseline, the baseline ships.

transcript.text: I am the head of marketing at a subscription company. The board asked for an AI segmentation of our customers, and I would like five or six segments with names we can put on a slide. The table I shared has one row per customer: signup date, the segment we already record, city, plan, tenure in months, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, and whether they churned the next month. Next quarter my team can run at most three email campaigns: one to move people to a higher plan, one to keep people who look likely to leave, and one welcome series for new customers. The same person should not receive two of them. My campaign managers will use the segments to decide who gets which campaign. [shares customers.csv]

Your board wants named segments, but the real job is routing: five or six groups that your campaign managers can point at three email campaigns without any customer landing in two queues.

**What needs care before any work is done**

1. **Your existing `segment` column is too coarse to build on.** It holds two values — business (239 customers, 14.6% churned next month) and consumer (961, 18.1%). It also correlates strongly with churn, so it can be a *descriptive* ingredient but not a target.
2. **`churned_next_month` must not be an input to the segments.** It is only known a month after the send. If a segment is defined using it, the managers could only assign it to customers whose future is already written — the slide would look sharp and the campaign would be impossible to run. I'll use it only to check which segments really do leave.
3. **City is a risky ingredient.** Grouping customers by city can quietly encode who lives there, and targeting or withholding offers on that basis can create problems you don't want in front of a board. I'd keep city out of the segment definition and use it only for reporting.
4. Upgrades can only be pitched to basic and plus, and the welcome series only to recent signups, so the three queues are structurally disjoint — good news for your no-overlap rule.
5. **Five or six names is a choice, not a finding.** I'll test more groupings and report where the names stop meaning something.

**The plan**

6. Fix the send-time rule set: which columns a manager can use the day they build the list (plan, tenure, spend, tickets, segment, signup date). Checked by confirming no customer's assignment needs future data.
7. Prepare the table: fill or flag missing `monthly_spend`, derive tenure bands and a "new customer" cut from `signup_date`. Checked by row counts before and after.
8. Find the groups from send-time behaviour, then name them. Checked against `churned_next_month`, spend and plan as a *validation* afterwards, not as an input.
9. Map segments to the three campaigns with an explicit precedence rule (at-risk beats upgrade, for instance) so no one appears twice; report how many customers each queue holds.
10. Produce the slide-ready names with definitions, sizes and one-line campaign rationale, plus the overlap check.

Stop when each of the 1,200 customers sits in exactly one named segment and one campaign queue, and the segment names hold up when tested against next-month churn.

If a step fails: if the groups won't separate cleanly on behaviour, I fall back to rule-based segments from plan, tenure and spend, and tell you plainly that the data does not support six distinct names.

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)

choices.what: Cluster customers on information available the day the list is built (plan, tenure, monthly spend, support tickets, your recorded segment, recency from signup date), keep city and churn out of the definition, then test the resulting groups against next-month churn and spend and write the slide names. You get: Five or six data-found segments with definitions and sizes, plus the check that each one behaves differently once you look at what happened next. Trade-off: The groups may come out as four or seven rather than exactly five or six, and the names have to follow the data, not the other way round. Two years ago we built a model that scores every new lead on how likely it is to become a customer, and the sales team calls the highest scores first. Since the autumn the sales team says the top leads are much worse than they used to be, and my manager wants me to retrain with a larger model and more features. Some context on the data: since the summer, part of our leads comes from a partner marketplace; we moved to a new CRM in August, and two form fields the model uses are no longer collected; and finance now counts a lead as converted when a free trial starts, where before it was the first payment. Before anything is built: I read this as a **drift diagnosis**, not a retraining job — and retraining first would likely make it worse.

**What I think is actually going on.** The sales team's complaint is about ranking quality: leads at the top of the list convert less often than they used to. Between summer and autumn four things changed, and three of them attack the ranking directly:

1. **The label changed.** "Converted" now means a free trial starts, not a first payment. Trial-start rate is higher, easier to reach, and ranked differently. If the old model was trained on payment and evaluation reports conversion, the two numbers aren't comparable — and if it's retrained on the new label while the training window still contains old-definition outcomes, the target is contaminated. A bigger model would fit that contamination more confidently, not less.
2. **Two input features stopped existing.** If the pipeline still serves them as null or median, every new lead's score shrinks toward the population mean, which produces exactly the symptom you describe: the top of the list is flatter, so the top decile is nearly a random sample. That's a serving bug, not a capacity problem.
3. **A new lead source arrived.** Marketplace leads are a different population, so their scores were never calibrated — the old model was fit on leads that came a different way. Adding "more features" doesn't fix a shifted input distribution.
4. **A CRM migration in August.** These usually change field semantics, timestamps and logging coverage, which can look like model decay.

Slowest to start, but it tells you which of the four causes you have. *Retrain on the new label and compare on a time-split:* fastest to satisfy your manager, but if the cause is (2), you will ship the same bug with a bigger footprint. *Manager brief only:* good politics, no facts.

I'd diagnose first. It's cheap and it changes what the retrain should even look like.

**The plan**

1. Export the two sets you named: the old training set as-is, and every lead since roughly June with: date created, lead source, whether it came via marketplace, all model inputs, the stored score, trial-start date, first-payment date. Check that scores are actually stored since August — if they aren't, I'll re-score the export with the old model instead.
2. Baseline the past: top-decile trial rate and payment rate by month, before and after August, as one line for each label, so the definition change is visible separately from any performance change.
3. Split the same by lead source, to see whether marketplace leads were ever in the model's training population and how their scores distribute.
4. Audit the two dropped fields: missing rate over time, and how much of the score's spread disappears when they go null.
5. Check calibration: predicted score versus actual rate, bucketed, per month and per source. Ranking loss plus flat calibration points to the feature problem; good calibration but lost ranking points to population shift.
6. Today a rulebook written by our underwriters approves about 40 percent of applications. Management wants to grow, so they asked me for a machine learning model that predicts default for every applicant, to replace the rulebook and approve more people safely. **What I think you actually need**

The request is “a model to replace the rulebook”, but the decision behind it is different: *how many more people can you approve before losses grow faster than the book*. Management wants to grow; the model is the instrument, not the answer. And once it decides each application automatically at the shop counter, the thing you manage is a **policy with thresholds**, not a score.

1. **Your evidence covers only the 40% you approved.** For everyone the rulebook declined you have no labels, so a model trained on this book is extrapolating precisely in the region growth would push you into — and it will look confident there. This is fixable, but by design (shadow mode, a small deliberate approval slice, a review band), not by a better algorithm. A model that “replaces the rulebook” on day one re-approves the reject region on faith.
2. **“Safely” is not a number yet.** Growth pays until the margin on a new loan stops covering its expected loss. Without your loss ceiling (and ideally average loan size, margin and recovery), no threshold can be set honestly — the same default rate is either fine or ruinous depending on pricing.
3. **Auto‑decline at the counter is an automated adverse decision.** That normally requires a stated reason and a route to contest it, and a bureau score as the main driver may be constrained. A human‑review band in the middle solves most of this, and most of the governance argument, at small cost.
4. **The rulebook is not a gold standard.** It approved some bad loans. Judging the model against it on the approved 40% measures who the rulebook already picked, not who repays.

**Three sound ways to start**, all using your export next week — I’d do the first, then the second, then the third:

- **Baseline first:** cut the 60,000 by bureau score band and rulebook outcome to see today's default rate and the headroom your current appetite allows. This is the number management asked for.
- **Scored model with a three‑zone policy** (auto‑approve / review / decline), trained and validated on the approved region, thresholds set from your loss ceiling.
- **Measured expansion:** model runs in shadow beside the rulebook, plus a small randomised approval slice in the reject region, so you earn labels where you have none and grow with a control group.

transcript.text: I am the commercial director of a building-materials distributor. Last year we bought a competitor, so we now have two customer lists: about 4,000 accounts in our system and 2,500 in theirs. I want a customer lifetime value model on the combined list so we know which accounts deserve a key-account manager; we can afford one for about 150 accounts. Each system has its own account numbers. Company names were typed by hand, the same contractor often has a separate account for each building site or branch, and many firms bought from both of us. Both systems hold three years of invoices with the account number, date and amount. Nothing is exported yet. My sales reps say the big customers are obvious and the list should find the ones they miss.

I've read this carefully, because what you've described is a different problem from the one you asked for — and the difference decides whether those 150 posts go to the right people.

A per-account CLV would systematically miss exactly the customers your reps say the list should find, and it would hand several of your 150 slots to branches of the same three builders.

**What needs care before any work.** First, the unit: value must be calculated at company level, with account detail kept underneath so a KAM walks in knowing which sites are which. Second, money: your invoices give date and amount, so this ranks revenue, not profit — and a builder's merchant selling commodity blocks alongside high-margin finishes doesn't earn the same on a pound. Third, consequence: a bad link moves a key account from one firm to another, so every merge needs a confidence score and your reps must vet the final list. Fourth, it must look forward, not only back — three years of history ranks last year's winners; the 150 slots are a bet on the next twelve months.

**How it could be solved.** Merge first, then model: most work up front, correct answer at the end (my choice). Or rank accounts as they stand today: fast, useful for one sanity check, wrong as a staffing basis. Or bolt on a name-matching tool later: cheaper, but the model inherits whatever the bad grouping did.

The plan:

1. You export both invoice tables plus the account/customer master from each system as CSV with headers. Checked by: account counts near 4,000 and 2,500, dates spanning three years.
2. We build one customer key per real company — name matching, plus any shared identifiers, flagging multi-site and cross-system duplicates.
3. Consolidate invoices to company level; baseline value, recency and trend. Checked by: totals reconciling against each system's own figures.
4. Predict next-year revenue per company, trained on the first two years and scored on the third as a holdout. Checked by: backtest error on that held-out year.
5. Rank to 150, and produce the gap list: firms that enter the top 150 only once their accounts are combined — the ones your reps miss today.

Stop when: the 150-company list plus gap list exists and your reps have reviewed a sample.
If a step fails: if matching proves too weak to link safely, we fall back to valuing each system separately and treat cross-system duplicates as a manually reviewed flag list.
